intake: spiritual-unaffiliated: Buddhist-leaning with a panpsychist streak; no personal God, mind is not an add-on to matter but the inside of it, the self is a process not a thing, raised Anglican in Nairobi and left it in my twenties

walk.note: That is how it went for me; the story arrived before the questions did.
Looking for God in the world rather than in the book is the honest next step once testimony is all you have.
The hiding-God dilemma is fair, and a first cause is not a God who answers anyone.
One prayer study is a thin plank, but the conclusion matches what I already hold: no prayer-answering God shows up where it should.
I grant that mind does not reduce to matter, but that gives you non-reduction, not two kinds of thing; one kind with an inside and an outside is still on the table.
Everything here shows mind depends on and changes with the brain; dependence is not identity, and 'the brain stores consciousness' assumes the thing being argued.
Widening matter to fields, energy and information is right, and it quietly makes room for what I believe.
Physics gives structure and not what has it, and the only inside we know directly is experience; this is my own view in the author's words, though I would not call it a dream.

'The brain is the only structure known to create consciousness' is exactly the premise Dream just loosened, and a dream does not need a dreamer; experience arises, as Lichtenberg's 'it thinks' says, and the author cites him and walks past him.
Granting a subject, Strawson's point carries; I would draw the circle wider than brains, but the direction is right.
Metta ahead of proof; I would make the same choice and the author is honest that it is one.
Care that stays open to correction is a good description of learned ignorance; the entropy aside is odd but does no harm.

The text lists equanimity as an open response and then takes hope without arguing against it; equanimity is the one I take, and the no-self view also doubts the premise that a being's good must be carried by that being persisting.
Religion2 is hope and fidelity, not hope toward a maker, and the move's own last sentence concedes that being a maker does not make a maker resolved.
'More of a bargain than an argument' gives me nothing to weigh; who is bargaining, and for what?

I can grant that a mind attending to everything has no one home, but that makes it not a subject, not nonexistent; 'both parties admitted' names no parties, and the text itself says Aquinas's knowing has not been shown incoherent.
Suffering is bad for the one who suffers whether or not anything stands behind it; this is close to the first noble truth and I take it gladly.
The author says the need to be remembered is a motive and not evidence, so what is left is a choice to hold the self apart; I would loosen that grip rather than hold it.
Stopping where there is no data is the right thing to do, and saying so is better than pretending.

first_exit.why: The move says the mind does not seem to reduce to matter, and I agree, but it jumps from that to two different kinds of thing when a single kind that has both a structure and an inside would explain the same seeming. Non-reduction is a reason to look again at what matter is, not a reason to double the inventory.

comment: You name equanimity as an open response at Ignorance2 and then take hope without saying a word against it, and from where I sit equanimity is what Mercy becomes when it stops needing anything to continue, so I would want to hear why hope outranks it for you rather than just that it does. Moves 14 to 16 are where the writing thins to a few lines each, and that is exactly where the route turns on its hardest premise. Also, you cite Lichtenberg twice and never answer him; a drummer knows the pulse is there before anyone is counting it.
